title: The Wednesday Class: rue Ballu, Fontainebleau, and the Century She Taught
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House on the rue La Bruyere

stops.name: 30 rue La Bruyere, Paris: born into the trade
stops.date_confidence: attested. The birth date is firm; the address is 30 rue La Bruyere, Paris 9e, per 9eme Histoire and Encyclopedia.com. Older biographies say Montmartre, meaning the Nouvelle Athenes quarter of the ninth arrondissement and not the butte, an ambiguity that has produced an 800 m error in more than one gazetteer.
stops.campa: At 30 rue La Bruyere in the ninth arrondissement a daughter is born to Ernest Boulanger, composer and professor of voice at the Conservatoire, born himself the year of Waterloo, and to Raissa Myshetskaya, thirty-one, a singer who claims descent from a Russian princely house. He is seventy-two. She was his pupil before she was his wife. Ernest still goes out to teach; the Conservatoire is a workplace in this household before it is anything else. The child is registered Juliette Nadia.
suggested_refs: The Boulanger household of the Nouvelle Athenes quarter, Paris 9e

stops.name: Paris: the fire bell
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and pinned at the canonical Paris centroid because no source records the street, the household address in that year, or the month. Her own retelling in Monsaingeon, whose preface warns that some passages are reconstructed from memory rather than transcribed.
stops.campa: She is about five when a fire engine passes in the street and the bell goes through her. Other children run to the window or hide. She goes to the piano and starts hunting the pitch, striking keys until she finds what she heard. Her parents watch her do it. In an apartment where music is the trade and the father is already old, this is the afternoon the household settles what the daughter is going to be. Neither the street nor the month is recorded, and the only source for any of it is her own telling, ninety years on.
stops.quote: One day I heard a fire bell. Instead of crying out and hiding, I rushed to the piano and tried to reproduce the sounds. My parents were amazed.
stops.quote_source: Bruno Monsaingeon, Mademoiselle: Conversations with Nadia Boulanger, trans. Robyn Marsack (Northeastern University Press, 1985), p. 20
suggested_refs: Monsaingeon, Mademoiselle (1985), the childhood chapters

stops.name: Paris: Lili
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date. The family address in August 1893 is not documented in reachable sources, so the stop takes the canonical Paris centroid rather than a street.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of August a second daughter is born, Marie-Juliette Olga, called Lili. Nadia is not quite six. The sister will be ill for most of her life, will compose before she is twenty, and in 1913 will take outright the prize Nadia competes for and does not win. From the beginning Nadia handles her: carries her to lessons, sits out the illnesses with her, reads to her. Lili will live twenty-four years. Nadia will live sixty-one more after her sister is dead.
suggested_refs: Lili Boulanger, Faust et Helene (1913) and the late choral works Nadia would spend her life programming

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris, rue du Conservatoire: admitted at nine
stops.date_confidence: contested year, month unknown. Wikipedia gives entry in 1896; Britannica's formal-training span runs 1897-1904 and the research pool's own geography lens carried 1897. Not resolved; dated 1896 to order the segment. The Conservatoire stood on the rue du Conservatoire until 1911, so this is the building, and it is the pin the atlas already uses for that address.
stops.campa: She enters the Conservatoire on the rue du Conservatoire at nine years old, into the building where her father has taught since long before she was born. The sources split on whether the year is 1896 or 1897, and no reachable register settles it. She is the youngest in the room by years. Solfege first, then harmony, organ, accompaniment, fugue, the whole ladder. Composition she studies with Gabriel Faure, who stands closer to the family than a professor usually does. Organ she studies with Charles-Marie Widor.
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire national de musique on the rue du Conservatoire, Paris 2e, before the 1911 move to the rue de Madrid

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris: four first prizes and Raoul Pugno
stops.date_confidence: attested for the prizes, 1903 in harmony and 1904 in organ, accompaniment and fugue; the July date is conventional for the Conservatoire concours and is used here to order the segment.
stops.campa: Her father dies in 1900, eighty-five years old, and the household closes around the mother and the two daughters. In 1903 she takes the first prize in harmony. In 1904 she takes three more at once, organ, accompaniment and fugue, and walks out of the Conservatoire at seventeen with nothing left in the building to win. The same year she meets Raoul Pugno, one of the great pianists in France, thirty-five years older than she is. They will write together until he dies, and nearly everything she composes carries both their names.
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire concours records for 1903 and 1904

stops.name: 36 rue Ballu, Paris: the class begins
stops.date_confidence: attested for the autumn of 1904; the day is not recorded. Coordinate taken from the French Wikipedia entry for the square, now 3, place Lili-et-Nadia-Boulanger, which supersedes the several conflicting pins circulating for this address.
stops.campa: In the autumn she begins taking pupils in the family apartment at 36 rue Ballu, at the corner of the rue de Vintimille, and sets aside Wednesday afternoons for a class in analysis and sight-singing. She is seventeen and her father is four years dead; the teaching is partly how the household eats. The Wednesday class will run, interrupted twice by wars, for something close to seventy-five years. The furniture barely changes. The score on the stand changes every week.
stops.quote: No-one is obliged to give lessons. It poisons your life if you give lessons and it bores you.
suggested_refs: The apartment at 36 rue Ballu, later bequeathed to the Institut de France
sources: Kimberly Francis (ed.), Nadia Boulanger and Her World, ch. '36 rue Ballu: A Multifaceted Place'

stops.name: Institut de France, Quai de Conti: the Second Grand Prix
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month of the concours result is not given in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: She competes at the Institut de France for the Prix de Rome, and in 1908 the cantata La Sirene takes the Second Grand Prix. It is as close as she comes; the First never arrives. The same year she and Raoul Pugno complete Les Heures claires, a song cycle published under both their names. She is twenty years old, a laureate with a full teaching week and an apartment class every Wednesday. Her sister Lili is fourteen, and it is Nadia who teaches her harmony.
suggested_refs: La Sirene (1908), cantata; Les Heures claires (1908), with Raoul Pugno

stops.name: Gargenville, Les Maisonnettes: the summers on the Seine
stops.date_confidence: traditional for the decade, 1900s-1910s; no single year is documented and 1910 is used to order the segment. Coordinate is 2 place Lili Boulanger, Gargenville, per OSM, the pool's own figures being some 3.5 km out.
stops.campa: Through the summers the family keeps Les Maisonnettes at Gargenville, above the Seine some forty kilometres downstream from Paris, with Raoul Pugno's house near enough to walk to. The commune will buy the house in 1998 and the French state will label it a Maison des Illustres in 2014, for the two sisters together. For now it is where the work gets done in July: Nadia teaching, arranging, copying, and Lili, whose health collapses in Paris winters, composing out in the garden.
suggested_refs: Les Maisonnettes, 2 place Lili Boulanger, Gargenville, labelled Maison des Illustres in 2014
sources: Ville de Gargenville, 'Les Maisonnettes, lieu de memoire et de culture emblematique'
Yvelines Tourisme, Maisons des Illustres list

stops.name: Paris: the conducting debut
stops.date_confidence: attested for April 1912 and for the Societe des Matinees Musicales; no reachable source names the hall or the day. Pinned at the canonical Paris centroid. The research pool had staged this at her apartment, which is wrong for a public concert.
stops.campa: In April she stands in front of the Societe des Matinees Musicales and conducts. No reachable source names the hall or the programme. She is twenty-four, eight years into the Wednesday class, and in France in 1912 the women who have held a baton over a professional ensemble can be counted without notes. She does not make a career of it for another twenty years. The next time an orchestra of any size plays under her she will be forty-nine, and the orchestra will be the London Philharmonic.
suggested_refs: The Societe des Matinees Musicales concert series, Paris, spring 1912

stops.name: Institut de France: Lili takes the prize outright
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the research pool gives 1913 only, and 5 July is the date standard accounts give for the announcement. Treated as attested-by-general-record rather than by a document read for this file.
stops.campa: The Academie announces that the First Grand Prix de Rome for composition has gone to Marie-Juliette Olga Boulanger, nineteen years old, for the cantata Faust et Helene. No woman has held it before. The French press treats it as a national event. Nadia, who took the Second Grand Prix in this building five years ago and never the First, has been drilling her sister in harmony and counterpoint since Lili was old enough to sit at a keyboard. The prize she could not win is won inside her own family, by a pupil she made.
suggested_refs: Lili Boulanger, Faust et Helene, Prix de Rome cantata, 1913

stops.name: 36 rue Ballu, Paris: La ville morte, unheard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the composition span 1909-1913 and for the aborted Opera-Comique premiere; December 1913 is used to place the finished score just before Pugno's death on 3 January 1914. The destruction of the orchestration in a bombed Normandy warehouse is attested but undated.
stops.campa: Between 1909 and 1913 she and Pugno write an opera together, La ville morte, on a libretto by Gabriele d'Annunzio. The Opera-Comique schedules it for 1914. Pugno dies on the third of January of that year, the theatres close for the war, and the premiere never happens. Later the orchestral score is destroyed when the Normandy warehouse holding it is bombed, and only the piano and vocal reduction survives. The first performance anywhere is given in 2023, a hundred and ten years after she finished it.
stops.quote: If there is one thing of which I am certain, it is that I wrote useless music.
suggested_refs: La ville morte, first performance and world-premiere recording by Neal Goren, Catapult Opera and the Talea Ensemble, 2023-2024, Pentatone 2024
sources: San Francisco Classical Voice, 'A Lost Opera From Teaching Legend Nadia Boulanger Resurfaces'

stops.name: Paris: the Comite Franco-Americain
stops.date_confidence: the research pool's chronology gave a bare 1914; standard accounts, with Blair Fairchild, place the founding in 1915, and Wikipedia frames the whole thing as her 1914-1918 war work. Dated 1915 here. No premises are named, so the canonical Paris centroid stands.
stops.campa: With the war on, she stops most public playing and builds a relief committee instead, the Comite Franco-Americain du Conservatoire National de Musique et de Declamation, run with the American composer Blair Fairchild. Money and parcels are raised in the United States for French musicians at the front and for their families. She is twenty-seven. It is the first time she organizes Americans on behalf of French music, and she will still be working the same correspondence and the same card index of names sixty years later.
suggested_refs: The Comite Franco-Americain du Conservatoire National de Musique et de Declamation, 1915-1918

stops.name: Mezy-sur-Seine: Lili dies at twenty-four
stops.date_confidence: attested. The research pool had placed the death in Paris; it was at Mezy-sur-Seine. Cause given here as intestinal tuberculosis, the contemporary and still standard attribution; Crohn's disease is a modern retrospective re-diagnosis and is named as such. Coordinate is the commune centroid.
stops.campa: Lili dies on the fifteenth of March at Mezy-sur-Seine, twenty-four years old, of the intestinal tuberculosis that has been killing her since childhood. Modern writers sometimes re-diagnose it at a hundred years' distance as Crohn's disease. From this month Nadia stops composing almost entirely and begins the other work: editing, publishing, programming and conducting Lili's music, for sixty-one years, wherever anybody will let her. The last pages of it she took down herself, at her sister's dictation.
suggested_refs: The Boulanger family tomb, Cimetiere de Montmartre, division 33, where Lili is laid in 1918
sources: National Arts Centre biography of Lili Boulanger

stops.name: Ecole normale de musique, boulevard Malesherbes: joining the faculty
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1919; the month is not recorded. Correction applied: she joined the faculty, she did not co-found the school, which was founded by Alfred Cortot and Auguste Mangeot. Coordinate is 114 bis boulevard Malesherbes, Paris 17e.
stops.campa: Alfred Cortot and Auguste Mangeot found the Ecole Normale de Musique on the boulevard Malesherbes in the year after the armistice, and she joins the faculty: harmony, counterpoint, analysis, organ, composition. She did not found the school, whatever the later summaries say. What she does is arrive with a method already fifteen years old and a private class already known across Paris, and set it down inside an institution that will start sending her its Americans. She is thirty-two.
suggested_refs: The Ecole Normale de Musique de Paris, founded 1919 by Alfred Cortot and Auguste Mangeot
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ecole Normale de Musique de Paris'

segments.name: Fontainebleau, and the Americans Who Came

stops.name: Chateau de Fontainebleau: the summer school for Americans
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1921 and for her engagement as professor of harmony under the first director, Charles-Marie Widor. The opening month is conventional for the summer session; the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: In the Louis XV wing of the royal chateau, in rooms built for a king's household, a summer school opens for American musicians, organized around French teaching. The Americans come because the war has made France the place a serious young musician goes, and they will keep coming for fifty-eight summers, broken only by the second war. Boulanger is engaged as professor of harmony, and she will be in the building for almost all of those summers. The first director is Charles-Marie Widor, who was her own organ professor at the Conservatoire.
suggested_refs: The Louis XV wing of the Chateau de Fontainebleau, home of the Conservatoire americain from 1921
sources: Fontainebleau Schools of Music and Fine Arts, 'History'

stops.name: Chateau de Fontainebleau: Aaron Copland, twenty years old
stops.date_confidence: attested that Copland was among the first-year students who studied with her at Fontainebleau in 1921; the month within that first summer is not documented.
stops.campa: Aaron Copland, twenty years old, out of Brooklyn, is in the first summer's intake. He sits in on her harmony class out of curiosity and stays three years. She is thirty-three when he walks in, and has been teaching for seventeen years. He is the first American of consequence to go through the room. The line he opens carries Virgil Thomson, Walter Piston, Roy Harris, Elliott Carter, David Diamond and dozens more into rue Ballu over the next four decades.
stops.quote: Nadia Boulanger knew everything there was to know about music; she knew the oldest and the latest music, pre-Bach and post-Stravinsky, and knew it cold.
stops.quote_source: Aaron Copland, 'The Teacher: Nadia Boulanger', in Copland on Music (New York: Pyramid, 1963), pp. 70-77; full sentence verified in The Harvard Crimson, 21 April 1962
suggested_refs: Copland's essay 'The Teacher: Nadia Boulanger', typescript at the Library of Congress, copland.writ0102.0
sources: Aaron Copland, Copland on Music (1963), pp. 70-77
The Harvard Crimson, 'To Organize Time: A Sketch of Nadia Boulanger', 21 April 1962

stops.name: Cherbourg: the Aquitania sails on Christmas Eve
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sailing of 24 December 1924 aboard RMS Aquitania and the arrival in New York on 31 December. The quay is not documented: the Gare Maritime Transatlantique was built 1928-1933 and did not exist, so passengers were tendered out from the older quay, and the coordinate is the harbour rather than a berth.
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve she boards the RMS Aquitania at Cherbourg for her first crossing to America and lands in New York on the last day of the year. In her luggage is the organ part of a symphony by a former pupil of twenty-four who has never had an orchestral work played anywhere. The transatlantic terminal that will one day make this port famous has not been built; passengers are still tendered out to the liners lying in the roads. She will sail home on the twenty-eighth of February.
suggested_refs: The RMS Aquitania, Cunard, on the winter New York run

stops.name: Aeolian Hall, New York: the Copland symphony, first performance anywhere
stops.date_confidence: attested. Correction applied: this was the world premiere, not the American premiere, and it is a separate event from the 24 December 1924 sailing with which the research pool had conflated it. Venue Aeolian Hall, 34 West 43rd Street.
stops.campa: At Aeolian Hall on West Forty-third Street, the New York Symphony Society under Walter Damrosch gives the first performance anywhere of Aaron Copland's Symphony for Organ and Orchestra, with Boulanger at the organ. The work is three years out of her harmony class. She has crossed four thousand miles to play a part in a pupil's piece rather than one of her own, a choice she made permanently in 1918 and does not revisit. The date is the eleventh of January 1925.
suggested_refs: Aaron Copland, Symphony for Organ and Orchestra (1924), premiered 11 January 1925

stops.name: Paris: George Gershwin asks for lessons
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia's bare 1927 is the outlier; Gershwin's Paris stay ran March to June 1928, and his own letter to Boulanger refers to having met her two years earlier, around 1926. No venue is documented, so the stop takes the canonical Paris centroid. The wording of her refusal is reported, not quoted from any transcript.
stops.campa: George Gershwin, in Paris for a season and already the composer of Rhapsody in Blue, comes asking for lessons. She listens to him and turns him down, telling him, by the accounts that survive, that she has nothing to give him that he does not already have. The refusal is repeated so often that it hardens into a proverb about her: that she could hear when a technique was finished. No reachable source records the room, the day within the spring, or what Gershwin said back.
stops.quote: I can't provide anyone with inventiveness, nor can I take it away; I can simply provide the liberty to read, to listen, to see, to understand.
suggested_refs: Gershwin's Paris letters of spring 1928; the An American in Paris chronology

stops.name: Queen's Hall, London: two firsts and six discs of Monteverdi
stops.date_confidence: the two firsts are attested, 1936 for the London Philharmonic and November 1937 for the complete Royal Philharmonic Society concert; Queen's Hall as the venue is tagged reconstruction in the research pool and no programme was reachable. Neither month is recorded for 1936. The Monteverdi discs are dated 1937 with the place given only as Paris or London.
stops.campa: At Queen's Hall she conducts the London Philharmonic, the first woman to do it, and comes back in November of the following year to conduct a complete concert of the Royal Philharmonic Society, again the first. She is forty-nine when the conducting career begins in earnest; the organist and the teacher have been in place for thirty years. Between the two concerts she records six sides of Monteverdi madrigals for His Master's Voice, music close to three hundred years old that almost nobody is performing, cut onto shellac for a general public.
stops.quote: A good waltz has just as much value to her as a good fugue, and this is because she judges a work solely on its aesthetic content.
stops.quote_source: Lennox Berkeley, 'Nadia Boulanger as Teacher', The Monthly Musical Record, January 1931
suggested_refs: The 1937 HMV Monteverdi madrigal sides, among the first commercial recordings of the repertoire

stops.name: Symphony Hall, Boston: the baton from Koussevitzky
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1938 and for Koussevitzky handing her the baton; the day is not recorded and February is the opening month of the tour. Tour length corrected: February to May 1938, about four months. Lecture counts conflict, one account giving forty concerts and sixty lectures, another over a hundred lectures; both are carried as approximate.
stops.campa: Serge Koussevitzky hands her the baton of the Boston Symphony Orchestra, and no woman has held it before. The concert falls in the middle of a tour running February to May, at Harvard, at Radcliffe, at Wellesley, at the Longy School, in a country she has been supplying with composers for seventeen years. How much of it she actually did is not settled: one account gives forty concerts and sixty lectures, another puts the lectures above a hundred. Both figures are carried here as approximate.
suggested_refs: The Boston Symphony Orchestra programme books for the 1937-1938 season

stops.name: Dumbarton Oaks, Washington: the Stravinsky premiere
stops.date_confidence: attested that she conducted the premiere of Stravinsky's Concerto in E flat in Washington in 1938; the research pool gives the year only, and 8 May at Dumbarton Oaks is the date standard accounts give. Treated as attested-by-general-record.
stops.campa: In the music room of a Georgetown estate, in front of an invited audience of the Blisses' guests, she conducts the first performance of Igor Stravinsky's Concerto in E flat, written for Robert and Mildred Bliss and named for their house. Stravinsky is ill in Paris and cannot come, and it is Boulanger he sends to the podium in his place. Eighteen months from now his family will be sheltering in her village. The piece is a concerto grosso for a chamber band, and the room was built for nothing louder.
stops.quote: I can tell whether a piece is well-made or not, and I believe that there are conditions without which masterpieces cannot be achieved, but I also believe that what defines a masterpiece cannot be pinned down.
suggested_refs: Igor Stravinsky, Concerto in E flat 'Dumbarton Oaks' (1938), commissioned by Robert and Mildred Bliss

stops.name: Carnegie Hall, New York: the New York Philharmonic
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1939; the month is not documented and February is used to order the season. Correction applied: the New York, Philadelphia and Washington firsts fall in 1939, not later in 1938 as the research pool's geography lens had them.
stops.campa: She conducts the New York Philharmonic at Carnegie Hall, the first woman to do so. It is the second of four American orchestras to hand a woman the baton for the first time inside two seasons: Boston last year under Koussevitzky, Philadelphia and Washington within weeks of this. She is fifty-one, and no American orchestra offers her a post, this year or any other. Across the same tour she gives, by her hosts' count, a hundred and two lectures in a hundred and eighteen days.
suggested_refs: The New York Philharmonic programme books for the 1938-1939 season

stops.name: Academy of Music, Philadelphia: Stokowski's orchestra under a harmony teacher
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1939; the month is not documented. Coordinate corrected to 240 South Broad Street.
stops.campa: The Philadelphia Orchestra, at the Academy of Music on South Broad Street, plays under her, the first woman it has done that for. The orchestra is Stokowski's instrument, tuned over two decades for a sound nobody else in America can produce, and it takes direction from a fifty-one-year-old French organ teacher who has never held a permanent post with any orchestra anywhere. She will never hold one. She has no contract here and nothing of her own on the programme.
suggested_refs: The Academy of Music, 240 South Broad Street, Philadelphia

stops.name: Washington: the National Symphony, the fourth first
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was the first woman to conduct the National Symphony Orchestra in 1939; the month is not documented. The venue is an inference, not a citation: no source found names DAR Constitution Hall for this concert, though it was the orchestra's home.
stops.campa: She conducts the National Symphony Orchestra in Washington, the fourth of the season's firsts and the last of them. She sails home in the spring with four American orchestras behind her and no post in any of them, then or later. Within seven months France will be at war with Germany. No reachable source names the hall she conducted in; Constitution Hall was the orchestra's home in 1939, and the concert is placed there by inference rather than by a programme.
suggested_refs: DAR Constitution Hall, 1776 D Street NW, home of the National Symphony Orchestra in 1939

stops.name: Gargenville: the school closes and the Stravinskys are in the village
stops.date_confidence: attested for the closure of the Fontainebleau conservatory at the outbreak of war and for the Stravinsky family sheltering at Gargenville in the same weeks; the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: War is declared, the Fontainebleau school shuts and the Americans go home. She withdraws to Les Maisonnettes at Gargenville, forty kilometres downstream from Paris, where Igor Stravinsky and his family are also sheltering: two households in one village through the phoney war. She teaches the few pupils left and goes on with the editing of Lili's music. In June the Germans take Paris. She stays on in the village another four months, and then leaves the country by way of Spain.
suggested_refs: Teaching Stravinsky: Nadia Boulanger and the Consecration of a Modernist Icon (Oxford Academic), ch. 'The War: 1940-1942'

stops.name: Barcelona: over the border with Lili's case
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1940 and for the meeting with Ethel Thurston in Barcelona; the day is not recorded. Madrid follows on the same overland route and is folded into this stop rather than staged separately.
stops.campa: She crosses into Spain carrying almost nothing: her papers and the overnight case that belonged to Lili, dead twenty-two years, which she has kept and will go on keeping. In Barcelona she finds Ethel Thurston, an American pupil, who attaches herself to the escape and does not leave her side again until New York. The reputation that filled Carnegie Hall eighteen months ago is worth nothing at a frontier post. They go on through Madrid, and she is fifty-three years old.
suggested_refs: The overland refugee route Barcelona to Madrid to Lisbon, autumn 1940

stops.name: Lisbon: the ship she does not take
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, as tagged in the research pool: the account of the Greek liner and the switch to the SS Excambion rests on one source and the Greek ship is not named. The day is not recorded.
stops.campa: At Lisbon she holds a first-class ticket on a Greek liner. Thurston argues her out of it and onto the American steamer Excambion instead, on the reasoning that an American hull will not be touched. Her luggage goes separately under Thurston's safer papers, because they are afraid it will be seized at the border. What she carries aboard is a temporary visitor's permit. One source says the Greek ship never reached America, and names neither the ship nor how anyone knew.
suggested_refs: The SS Excambion on the Lisbon to New York run, autumn 1940

stops.name: New York: landing on a visitor's permit
stops.date_confidence: attested for 6 November 1940. Pinned at the canonical New York centroid; the pier is not documented.
stops.campa: She lands in New York on the sixth of November on a temporary visitor's permit, fifty-three years old, with no post, no apartment, no instrument of her own and no date for going back. Within weeks she has work; within two years she has posts in two cities. The country is full of former pupils who are now heads of department and directors of schools, and they place her: twenty years of Fontainebleau summers, paying out. She goes home in the first January she can, which is 1946.
suggested_refs: Boulanger's American teaching network, 1921-1940, as the mechanism of her wartime placement

stops.name: Longy School, 1 Follen Street, Cambridge: the war years
stops.date_confidence: attested for the span 1940-1945 by Longy's own history page; the month of her first class is not recorded and January 1941 orders the segment. Coordinate corrected: Longy stood at 1 Follen Street in these years, not at the present 27 Garden Street campus.
stops.campa: At the Longy School, then on Follen Street in Cambridge, she teaches harmony, fugue, counterpoint and advanced composition through the war years, and lectures in public on Beethoven's quartets and Bach's cantatas to rooms of Americans while Paris is under occupation. She keeps French hours and French standards and softens neither. The lectures are not consolation and are not offered as consolation. Longy's own history gives the span as 1940 to 1945.
stops.quote: Anyone who acts without paying attention to what he is doing is wasting his life. I'd go so far as to say that life is denied by lack of attention, whether it be to cleaning windows or trying to write a masterpiece.
suggested_refs: The Longy School of Music at 1 Follen Street, Cambridge, its address during the Boulanger years

stops.name: Peabody Conservatory, Baltimore: the second post
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1942; the month is not recorded. Coordinate corrected to the Peabody Institute on East Centre Street.
stops.campa: She adds the Peabody Conservatory in Baltimore to a load that already includes Longy, and commutes between the two cities, a woman in her middle fifties on American wartime trains. Radcliffe and Wellesley take her for lectures too, as they did on the 1938 tour. She has no country to go home to and fills the space with teaching hours, which is what she did in 1914 and what she will still be doing at ninety. She composes nothing at all in these years.
suggested_refs: The Peabody Institute, East Centre Street, Baltimore

stops.name: 36 rue Ballu, Paris: the Wednesday resumes
stops.date_confidence: attested for January 1946; the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: She is back in Paris in January, in the same apartment, and the Wednesday class resumes as though the interruption had been a long weekend. The room is unchanged: two pianos, the portraits, the score on the stand. What has changed is the traffic. From now until she dies, everybody comes here: conductors passing through, students on grants, composers stuck in a second movement, and the Americans, always the Americans. The queue does not break again for thirty-three years.
suggested_refs: The Wednesday class at 36 rue Ballu, resumed January 1946
sources: Kimberly Francis (ed.), Nadia Boulanger and Her World

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris, rue de Madrid: professor of accompaniment
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1946 appointment and for the tenure running to 1957; the month is not recorded and October orders the academic year. Coordinate note: the Conservatoire moved from the rue du Conservatoire to 14 rue de Madrid in 1911, so the 1946 chair is pinned there and not at the building of her own studies. This departs deliberately from the pin the atlas interlock carried for this stop.
stops.campa: The Conservatoire, which gave her every prize it had and then no chair for forty-two years, appoints her professor of accompaniment. She is fifty-nine. The building is the one on the rue de Madrid now, not the one she entered at nine. Michel Legrand arrives the same year, stays seven, and never wins a first prize; his own account of it, given long afterward, is that the pupils she meant to keep were the ones she gave nothing to. She holds the chair until 1957.
stops.quote: Anyone who allowed her in any piece to tell him what to do next would see that piece ruined before his eyes by the application of routine recipes and bromides from standard repertory.
stops.quote_source: Virgil Thomson, cited in Ned Rorem, 'The Composer and the Music Teacher', The New York Times, 23 May 1982
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire national superieur de musique at 14 rue de Madrid, Paris 8e

stops.name: Chateau de Fontainebleau: resident director
stops.date_confidence: contested year. Robert Casadesus ceded the Resident Director post to her in 1949 and she held it until her death, thirty years; English Wikipedia's 1953 refers to the direction of the whole Fontainebleau School, music and fine arts together; Britannica's 1950 is unsupported by the institutional sources and is dropped; the afterlife lens carried 1948. Ordered, not resolved.
stops.campa: Robert Casadesus hands her the resident directorship of the Conservatoire americain, and she takes charge of the school she has taught in since its first summer. She will run it for thirty years, until the year she dies. In 1953 the direction of the whole Fontainebleau establishment, music and fine arts together, comes to her as well. The sources give the first appointment as 1948, 1949, 1950 and 1953 depending on which office they mean; the school's own record says Casadesus ceded the post in 1949.
stops.quote: When you are writing music of your own, never strain to avoid the obvious.
stops.quote_source: Robin Orr, 'Boulanger', The Musical Times, March 1983
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire americain de Fontainebleau, directed by Boulanger 1949-1979
sources: Fontainebleau Schools of Music and Fine Arts, 'History'

stops.name: 36 rue Ballu, Paris: Astor Piazzolla plays a tango
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1954 and for the French government scholarship; the month is not recorded. The dialogue is reconstruction: two source strands exist and are incompatible. One quotes Piazzolla's own recollection of her words and names no piece; the other names the tango Triunfal and gives no quotation. They are not fused here, and the Gorin memoir is cited without a page because the page could not be read.
stops.campa: A thirty-three-year-old Argentine arrives on a French government grant with a case full of symphonies and hides what he actually does for a living, which is play the bandoneon in the tango cabarets of Buenos Aires. She reads the symphonies and tells him she cannot find him anywhere in them. Pressed, he admits the tango, and she makes him play it. What he goes home and builds out of that afternoon is nuevo tango. At the piano he gets a few bars in before she takes his hands and stops him.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Nadia Boulanger in Piazzolla's own recollection, quoted by Timothy Judd, 'Astor Piazzolla at 100', thelistenersclub.com, 17 March 2021; also recounted in Natalio Gorin, Astor Piazzolla: A Memoir, trans. Fernando Gonzalez (Amadeus Press, 2001)
suggested_refs: Piazzolla's Paris year, 1954-1955, and the sextet writing that follows his return to Buenos Aires
sources: La Nacion, 'El bandoneonista y su celebre maestra'
Timothy Judd, 'Astor Piazzolla at 100', thelistenersclub.com, 17 March 2021

stops.name: Saint Nicholas Cathedral, Monaco: the wedding music
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date of the religious ceremony and for her organizing the music. The detail that she chose only dead composers to avoid slighting living ones comes from the LA Phil's programme essay and is a widely repeated account rather than a documented instruction.
stops.campa: She organizes the music for the wedding of Prince Rainier III and Grace Kelly in the cathedral of Saint Nicholas, in front of six hundred guests and a television audience. Her answer to the problem of which living composer to honour is to honour none of them: every piece on the order of service is by a man already dead, so that nobody alive can count himself passed over. The detail comes from a programme essay rather than from any instruction of hers that survives.
suggested_refs: The order of service for the wedding of Rainier III and Grace Kelly, 19 April 1956
sources: Wikipedia, 'Wedding of Rainier III, Prince of Monaco, and Grace Kelly'
LA Phil, 'Get to Know: The Boulangers'

stops.name: Ankara: touring with Idil Biret
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1962; no month is recorded and the tour covered more than one city. Pinned at Ankara, the capital that hosted her.
stops.campa: She tours Turkey with Idil Biret, her pupil since the girl was a child: Boulanger conducts, Biret plays. She is seventy-five and the protegee is twenty-one. The older musician stands in front of the orchestra so the younger one can be heard, which is the arrangement she has been making since 1913, when the younger one was her own sister. The Turkish state receives her like visiting royalty, with a lady-in-waiting attached to her and rooms in the best hotels.
suggested_refs: Idil Biret Education Initiative, essays on her studies with Nadia Boulanger
sources: Idil Biret Education Initiative, essay excerpts on Nadia Boulanger

stops.name: The White House, Washington: Kennedy's invitation
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1962; no date within the year is recorded in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: John F. Kennedy invites her to the White House. She is seventy-five and has been coming to the United States for thirty-eight years: first as a curiosity, then as the conductor who broke the same barrier on four podiums in two seasons, then as a refugee on a temporary permit teaching harmony in Cambridge. Now the President of the United States asks her to dinner. No reachable source records the date within the year, the occasion, or what was played.
suggested_refs: The Kennedy White House musical programme, 1961-1963

stops.name: 36 rue Ballu, Paris: Philip Glass on a Fulbright
stops.date_confidence: attested for the span 1964-1966 on a Fulbright; the month of his arrival is not recorded.
stops.campa: Philip Glass, twenty-seven, arrives from New York on a Fulbright and finds himself doing species counterpoint and figured bass like a first-year student. He stays two years. What she gives him is not a style, which he would have refused, but a way of hearing what holds a piece together, and he goes on saying so for the next sixty years. She takes him the way she took Copland in 1921, by working out first what is already in him. She is seventy-seven.
stops.quote: You need an established language and then, within that established language, the liberty to be yourself. It's always necessary to be yourself, that is a mark of genius in itself.
stops.quote_source: Paul Driver, review 'Mademoiselle', Tempo, June 1986, pp. 33-34
suggested_refs: Kimberly Francis (ed.), Nadia Boulanger and Her World, ch. '36 rue Ballu: A Multifaceted Place'
sources: Kimberly Francis (ed.), Nadia Boulanger and Her World

stops.name: Moscow Conservatory: the Tchaikovsky jury
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1966; the competition ran in the summer and no exact date is given in the reachable sources. Coordinate is the canonical atlas pin for the Moscow Conservatory on Bolshaya Nikitskaya. Correction applied: the Great Hall was built in 1901 and was not built for Tchaikovsky, who died in 1893.
stops.campa: She sits on the jury of the International Tchaikovsky Competition in the Moscow Conservatory, in the building where Tchaikovsky himself taught harmony for twelve years in the 1860s and 1870s, before either the great hall or the competition existed. She is seventy-eight, French, Catholic, and voting on Soviet pianists in the middle of the Cold War. In the same years she is also teaching at the Yehudi Menuhin School, the Royal College of Music and the Royal Academy in London.
suggested_refs: The 1966 International Tchaikovsky Competition, Moscow

stops.name: 36 rue Ballu, Paris: the camera, and the singing at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was filmed in the apartment in early 1976 and that pupils sang to her in her last months. The film's own chronology is internally inconsistent in the sources: material described as shot in the late 1960s and early 1970s is also described as showing her in her late eighties, which cannot both hold, since she turned eighty in 1967. Left unresolved and no age is asserted here.
stops.campa: Bruno Monsaingeon sets a camera up in the apartment and films the Wednesday class, a lesson on Schumann's Davidsbundlertanze among the material, and cuts it into a portrait released the following year. It is the only moving record of how the class ran. Her health is going. In the last months she will not be able to teach and the pupils will come anyway, sitting in this room singing Schubert and Schumann and Mozart to her, while others stand out in the street because there is no room left inside.
suggested_refs: Bruno Monsaingeon, Mademoiselle: Nadia Boulanger (1977), his first film
sources: IMDb and MUBI listings for Nadia Boulanger: Mademoiselle (1977)

stops.name: Chateau de Fontainebleau, the English Garden: ninety years old
stops.date_confidence: attested for 13 August 1977 for the birthday celebration, and for 9 February 1977 for the Legion d'honneur, which is folded into this stop rather than staged separately in Paris.
stops.campa: In February the President of the Republic makes her a Grand Officer of the Legion d'honneur. In August the school gathers in the English Garden of the chateau for her ninetieth birthday, students out of six decades standing about on the grass, some of them past seventy themselves. She has directed this place for twenty-eight years and taught in it for fifty-six. She is nearly blind and still takes the Wednesday class in Paris. The photographs from that afternoon show her seated, upright, listening.
suggested_refs: The English Garden of the Chateau de Fontainebleau, site of the 1977 ninetieth-birthday gathering

stops.name: Paris: the twenty-second of October
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date. No address is given for the death in the reachable sources, so the canonical Paris centroid stands. The two pupil totals are not rival estimates: about twelve hundred is the career figure, over two hundred and fifty counts notable students only.
stops.campa: She dies on the twenty-second of October, ninety-two years old, brought back from Fontainebleau to Paris by ambulance some weeks before as her condition worsened. She has taught for seventy-five years. The Wednesday class had run since the autumn of 1904, through two wars and one exile, and it stops now. Those who have tried to total the pupils put the career figure at about twelve hundred, of whom more than two hundred and fifty are names the world has heard. She stopped composing in March 1918 and never took it up again.
suggested_refs: The Washington Post obituary, 'Nadia Boulanger Dies', October 1979

stops.name: Cimetiere de Montmartre: division 33, the family tomb
stops.date_confidence: the grave and the division are attested; the burial date is not documented and is placed a few days after the death of 22 October, so the figure is inferred. The posthumous facts named in the prose are attested: the bequest to the Institut de France, the square named for Lili alone on 5 May 1970 and renamed for both sisters on 19 November 2021.
stops.campa: She is buried in the Cimetiere de Montmartre, division 33, in the family tomb, beside Ernest dead seventy-nine years and beside Lili dead sixty-one. The burial date is not documented and is placed here a few days after the death. The apartment on the rue Ballu goes to the Institut de France. The square outside it had carried Lili's name alone since 1970; in November 2021 the city adds Nadia's, and the address becomes 3, place Lili-et-Nadia-Boulanger.
stops.quote: A one-woman graduate school so powerful and so permeating that legend credits every American town with two things, a five-and-dime and a Boulanger pupil.
stops.quote_source: Virgil Thomson, oft-quoted; attribution confirmed in the JAMS review of Nadia Boulanger and Her World
suggested_refs: The Boulanger family tomb, Cimetiere de Montmartre, division 33
